summary: An operating system is a program that sits between the user and the computer hardware. It controls how every other program runs and performs the basic tasks: memory, processor, device and file management, plus security and error handling.
Popular examples are Linux, Windows, VMS, OS/400, AIX and z/OS.

Each function follows the same pattern: keep track of a resource, decide who gets it and for how long, allocate it, and take it back when it is no longer needed. Once you see that pattern, the rest of the course is variations on it.

items: An operating system, or OS, is an interface between a computer user and the computer hardware. It is software that performs the basic tasks: file management, memory management, process management, handling input and output, and controlling peripheral devices such as disk drives and printers.
Popular operating systems include Linux, Windows, VMS, OS/400, AIX and z/OS.

The tutorial's definition is short and worth remembering. An operating system is a program that acts as an interface between the user and the computer hardware, and controls the execution of all kinds of programs.

Here are its important functions. Memory management, processor management, device management and file management. Then security, control over system performance, job accounting, error detecting aids, and coordination between other software and users.
We will spend a chapter or more on each of the big four, so this chapter only sketches them.

Memory management is about primary memory, also called main memory. Main memory is a large array of words or bytes where each word or byte has its own address. It is fast storage that the CPU accesses directly, and for a program to run, it must be in main memory.

For memory, the OS keeps track of which parts are in use and by whom. In multiprogramming it decides which process gets memory, when, and how much. It allocates memory when a process asks, and de-allocates it when the process no longer needs it or has terminated.
Processor management matters in a multiprogramming environment, where the OS decides which process gets the processor and for how much time. This function is called process scheduling.
The OS keeps track of the processor and the status of each process; the program responsible is known as the traffic controller.
It allocates the CPU to a process and de-allocates it when the process is no longer required.

Device management works through drivers. The OS keeps track of all devices; the program responsible is the I/O controller. It decides which process gets a device, when and for how long, allocates the device in the most efficient way, and de-allocates it afterwards.

File management starts from the idea that a file system is normally organized into directories, which may contain files and other directories. The OS keeps track of information, location, use and status of files. These facilities are collectively known as the file system.
It decides who gets resources, allocates them and de-allocates them.

Then there are other important activities. Security prevents unauthorized access to programs and data by means of passwords and similar techniques. Control over system performance records delays between a request for a service and the response.

Job accounting tracks time and resources used by jobs and users. Error detecting aids produce dumps, traces and error messages. And the OS coordinates compilers, interpreters, assemblers and other software among users.

Notice the pattern. For memory, processor, devices and files the OS does the same four things: it keeps track of the resource, decides who gets it, allocates it, and takes it back. When you meet a new OS topic later, ask which of these four steps it is about.

A tiny Python model of the pattern follows. It is a memory ledger: allocate gives a process some memory, free takes it back. The practice section asks you to finish it, and you can run the Python on this device.

summary: Operating systems have evolved with each computer generation. The tutorial describes five types: batch, time-sharing, distributed, network and real-time systems.

In a batch system the user does not interact with the computer. Similar jobs are grouped and run together, so the CPU is often idle waiting for slow mechanical I/O. Time-sharing lets many users share one machine, switching so fast that each gets quick responses.

Distributed systems spread work over several loosely coupled processors. Network operating systems run on a server and share files and printers. Real-time systems must respond within fixed time limits, hard or soft.

Real-time examples: industrial control, medical imaging, air traffic control, robots.

items: Operating systems have been around since the very first computer generation, and they keep evolving. This chapter covers the most common types.

First, the batch operating system. Users do not interact with the computer directly. Each user prepares a job on an off-line device like punch cards and submits it to the computer operator. To speed up processing, jobs with similar needs are batched together and run as a group.
The operator sorts programs with similar requirements into batches.

Batch systems have three problems. There is no interaction between the user and the job. The CPU is often idle, because mechanical I/O devices are slower than the CPU. And it is difficult to give jobs the priority they want.

Second, time-sharing systems. Time-sharing lets many people at different terminals use one computer at the same time. It is also called multitasking, a logical extension of multiprogramming. The processor's time is shared among the users.
The difference from a multiprogrammed batch system is the goal. Multiprogrammed batch maximizes processor use. Time-sharing minimizes response time.

The CPU switches between jobs so frequently that the user gets an immediate response. In transaction processing, each user program runs in a short burst, or quantum, of computation. If n users are present, each gets a quantum, and the response time is a few seconds at most.

Time-sharing has advantages: quick response, no duplication of software, and less CPU idle time. It has disadvantages too: reliability problems, questions of security and integrity of user programs and data, and problems of data communication.

Third, the distributed operating system. Distributed systems use multiple central processors to serve multiple real-time applications and users. Jobs are distributed among the processors. The processors talk to each other over communication lines such as buses or telephone lines.
These are called loosely coupled systems.
Processors in a distributed system can vary in size and function. They are called sites, nodes or computers.

The advantages: a user at one site can use resources at another; data exchange speeds up, for example by email; if one site fails the others can carry on; service to customers is better; and the load on the host computer and delays in processing are reduced.

Fourth, the network operating system. It runs on a server and gives the server the ability to manage data, users, groups, security, applications and other networking functions. Its main purpose is to allow shared file and printer access among multiple computers, typically in a local area network.
The tutorial's examples include Windows Server 2003 and 2008, UNIX, Linux, Mac OS X, Novell NetWare and BSD.

Network operating systems offer centralized and stable servers, server-managed security, easy upgrades, and remote access. The costs are a high price to buy and run a server, dependence on a central location, and regular maintenance and updates.

Fifth, the real-time operating system. A real-time system processes and responds to inputs so fast that it controls the environment. The time to respond is called the response time. Real-time systems are used when there are rigid time requirements on a processor or on the flow of data.
A real-time OS must have well-defined, fixed time constraints, otherwise the system fails. Examples are scientific experiments, medical imaging, industrial control, robots and air traffic control.
There are two kinds. Hard real-time systems guarantee that critical tasks complete on time; secondary storage is limited or missing, data is kept in ROM, and virtual memory is almost never found.
Soft real-time systems are less restrictive: a critical task gets priority and keeps it until it completes. Examples are multimedia, virtual reality and planetary rovers.

To feel the difference between batch and time-sharing, simulate them. The Python below runs jobs in submission order, as a batch would. In the practice section you will group similar jobs into batches, which is what the operator did.

summary: An operating system provides services both to the programs that run on it and to the users who run them. The tutorial lists seven: program execution, I/O operations, file system manipulation, communication, error detection, resource allocation and protection.

Program execution means loading a program, running it, and offering process synchronization, communication and deadlock handling. File services decide which program may read or write which file. Communication between processes uses shared memory or message passing.
Errors are detected and handled so computing stays correct. Resources are allocated by schedulers. Protection controls access to resources, authenticating users by passwords.

items: An operating system provides services to both users and programs. It gives programs an environment to execute in, and it gives users convenient ways to run them.
The common services are program execution, I/O operations, file system manipulation, communication, error detection, resource allocation and protection.

Program execution. Operating systems handle many kinds of activities, from user programs to system programs like the printer spooler, name servers and file servers. Each of these activities is encapsulated as a process.
A process includes the complete execution context: the code to execute, the data to manipulate, the registers and the OS resources in use.

With respect to program management the OS loads a program into memory, executes it, handles its execution, and provides mechanisms for process synchronization, process communication and deadlock handling.

I/O operation. An I/O subsystem comprises I/O devices and their driver software. Drivers hide the peculiarities of specific hardware from users. The OS manages communication between the user and the drivers.
An I/O operation means a read or write on a file or on a specific I/O device, and the OS gives access to the device when it is required.

File system manipulation. A file is a collection of related information. Files are stored on secondary storage for the long term: magnetic tape, magnetic disk, and optical disks like CD and DVD. Each medium has its own speed, capacity, transfer rate and access method.
A file system is organized into directories.

Here is what the OS does for files. A program needs to read or write a file. The OS gives the program permission for the operation, and permission varies from read-only to read-write to denied. The OS provides interfaces to create and delete files and directories, and to back up the file system.

Communication. In distributed systems, which are collections of processors that share no memory, peripherals or clock, the OS manages communication between processes. Two processes often need to exchange data. They may be on one computer or on different computers connected by a network.
Communication is implemented in two ways: shared memory or message passing.

Error handling. Errors can occur anywhere: in the CPU, in I/O devices or in memory hardware. The OS constantly checks for possible errors and takes appropriate action to ensure correct and consistent computing.

Resource management. In a multi-user or multitasking environment, resources such as main memory, CPU cycles and file storage must be allocated to each user or job. The OS manages all kinds of resources using schedulers, and CPU scheduling algorithms are used for better utilization of the CPU.

Protection. With multiple users and concurrent processes, processes must be protected from each other's activities. Protection is a way to control the access of programs, processes or users to resources.
The OS ensures that all access is controlled, that external I/O devices are protected from invalid access attempts, and that users are authenticated, for example by passwords.

File permission is a clean example of protection plus a service. The practice section has you write the check that decides whether a user may read or write a file, using the permissions idea from this chapter.

summary: This chapter covers the properties an operating system can have: batch processing, multitasking, multiprogramming, interactivity, real-time operation, a distributed environment and spooling.

Multiprogramming keeps several jobs in memory so the CPU always has one to run, which raises CPU utilization but requires CPU scheduling and memory management. Multitasking adds rapid switching so users interact with each program while it runs.
Spooling, short for simultaneous peripheral operations on line, puts the data of I/O jobs in a buffer so slow devices can catch up while the CPU keeps computing.

keyPoints: Batch: jobs run in submission order; when one finishes its memory is released and output goes to a spool.

items: This chapter looks at properties of operating systems. Several of them extend ideas from chapter 2, but here we see what the OS actually does for each.

Batch processing is a technique where the OS collects programs and data together in a batch before processing starts. The OS defines a job with a predefined sequence of commands, programs and data as one unit.
It keeps a number of jobs in memory and executes them without manual intervention, in the order of submission, first come first served.

When a job completes, its memory is released and its output is copied into an output spool for later printing or processing. The advantages: much of the operator's work moves to the computer, and a new job starts as soon as the previous one finishes.
The disadvantages: programs are difficult to debug, a job could enter an infinite loop, and without protection one batch job can affect pending jobs.
Multitasking is when multiple jobs are executed by the CPU simultaneously by switching between them. Switches occur so frequently that users can interact with each program while it is running.
Multitasking systems are also called time-sharing systems, developed to provide interactive use of a computer at reasonable cost.

A time-shared OS uses CPU scheduling and multiprogramming to give each user a small portion of the CPU. Each user has at least one separate program in memory. A program that is loaded and executing is a process. A process typically runs only a short time before it finishes or needs I/O.

Interactive I/O is slow, so it may take a long time to complete. During this time the CPU can be used by another process. Since each command in a time-shared system tends to be short, only a little CPU time is needed per user.
As the CPU switches rapidly from one user to the next, each user is given the impression of having their own CPU.

Multiprogramming is sharing the processor when two or more programs reside in memory at the same time. It assumes a single shared processor. It increases CPU utilization by organizing jobs so the CPU always has one to execute.
The OS keeps several jobs in memory, a subset of the job pool, picks one and begins to execute it.

When the running job waits, for example for I/O, the OS switches to another. Multiprogramming OSs monitor the state of all active programs and system resources using memory management programs, so that the CPU is never idle unless there are no jobs.
Advantages: high CPU utilization, and the feeling that many programs get the CPU almost simultaneously. Disadvantages: CPU scheduling is required, and memory management is required to hold many jobs.

Interactivity is the ability of users to interact with the system. The OS provides an interface, manages input devices such as the keyboard and output devices such as the monitor. Since the user submits a request and waits for the result, the response time must be short.

Real-time systems are usually dedicated, embedded systems. The OS typically reads from and reacts to sensor data, and must guarantee a response to events within fixed periods of time to ensure correct performance.

A distributed environment means multiple independent CPUs or processors. The OS distributes computation among several physical processors. They share no memory or clock; each has its own local memory. They communicate through various communication lines, and the OS manages that communication.

Spooling is an acronym for simultaneous peripheral operations on line. It puts the data of various I/O jobs in a buffer, a special area in memory or on disk that I/O devices can access. The OS handles spooling because devices have different data access rates.

The spool buffer is a waiting station where data can rest while the slower device catches up. Because of spooling the computer can perform I/O in parallel: read from tape, write to disk and write to a printer while it is computing.

The advantages of spooling: a disk becomes a very large buffer, and I/O for one job overlaps with processor work for another job. Here is a tiny spooling model in Python; the practice section asks you to complete it.

# jobs: [name, arrival, print_time]  (one printer, first come first served)

for name, arrival, dur in [["A", 0, 3], ["B", 1, 2]]:
    t = max(t, arrival) + dur
    print(name, "finishes at", t)     # A at 3, B at 5

practice.title: Printer spooler
practice.intro: One printer serves jobs first come first served. Write spool(jobs). Each job is [name, arrival, print_time]. Jobs are given in order of arrival. Return a list of [name, finish_time]. The printer may sit idle until a job arrives.
practice.hint: Keep a clock t. For each job, start = max(t, arrival), then t = start + print_time.
practice.solution:
def spool(jobs):
    t = 0
    out = []
    for name, arrival, dur in jobs:
        t = max(t, arrival) + dur
        out.append([name, t])
    return out

summary: A process is a program in execution: the basic unit of work in the system. A program is passive code; a process is its dynamic instance.

In memory a process has four sections: stack for function parameters, return addresses and local variables, heap for memory allocated at run time, text for the code and current activity, and data for global and static variables.
A process passes through five states: start, ready, running, waiting and terminated. The OS tracks each process in a process control block, identified by an integer process ID.

items: A process is basically a program in execution. Its execution must progress in a sequential fashion. A process is the entity that represents the basic unit of work implemented in the system.
In simple terms: we write programs in a text file, and when we execute the program it becomes a process which performs the tasks mentioned in the program.
When a program is loaded into memory and becomes a process, it can be divided into four sections: stack, heap, text and data.
The stack contains temporary data such as method or function parameters, the return address and local variables. The heap is memory dynamically allocated to the process during its run time.
The text section includes the current activity, represented by the value of the program counter and the contents of the processor's registers. The data section contains global and static variables.

A program is a piece of code, from a single line to millions of lines, written by a programmer in some programming language. A program is a collection of instructions that performs a specific task when executed. Compared with a program, a process is a dynamic instance of that program.
The tutorial also gives definitions around it. A part of a program that performs a well-defined task is an algorithm. A collection of programs, libraries and related data is software.

Now the process life cycle. When a process executes, it passes through different states. These stages may differ between operating systems, and their names are not standardized. In general a process is in one of five states.

Start is the initial state, when the process is first created. Ready means the process is waiting to be assigned to a processor. A process comes to ready after start, or when the scheduler interrupts it so the CPU can go to another process.

Running: once the OS scheduler assigns the processor, the state is running and the processor executes its instructions. Waiting: the process moves to waiting if it needs a resource, such as user input or a file to become available.
Terminated: when it finishes, or the OS terminates it, it waits to be removed from main memory.
For every process the OS keeps a data structure called the process control block, or PCB. It is identified by an integer process ID, the PID. It keeps all the information needed to track the process.

A PCB records: the process state, process privileges, the process ID, a pointer to the parent process, the program counter, the CPU registers, CPU scheduling information such as priority, memory management information such as page tables and limits, accounting information such as CPU time used, and I/O status information such as the devices allocated.

The architecture of a PCB depends completely on the operating system and may contain different information in different systems. The PCB is maintained for the process throughout its lifetime and deleted once the process terminates.

The state machine is easy to simulate. Here is the transition rule in Python. In the practice section you will write the function that walks a process through events and tells you which states it visited.

The OS keeps PCBs in queues: a job queue of all processes, a ready queue of processes in memory waiting for the CPU, and device queues of processes blocked on I/O. A process moves between queues as its state changes.

Three schedulers act at different speeds: the long-term job scheduler admits jobs, the short-term CPU scheduler picks the next process to run, and the medium-term scheduler swaps processes out and back in. A context switch saves one process's state in its PCB and loads another's.

items: Process scheduling is the activity of the process manager that handles removing the running process from the CPU and selecting another process, based on a particular strategy.
It is an essential part of multiprogramming operating systems, which load more than one process into memory at a time and share the CPU by time multiplexing.

The OS keeps all PCBs in process scheduling queues. It maintains a separate queue for each process state, and the PCBs of all processes in the same state sit in the same queue. When a process changes state, its PCB is unlinked from its current queue and moved to the queue for its new state.

Three queues matter most. The job queue keeps all the processes in the system. The ready queue keeps all processes in main memory that are ready and waiting to execute; a new process is always put here. Device queues hold processes blocked because an I/O device is unavailable.

The OS can use different policies to manage each queue: first in first out, round robin, priority and so on. The scheduler then decides how to move processes between the ready queue and the run queue, which can hold only one entry per processor core.

A simple model has two states: running and not running. A new process enters as running. Processes that are not running wait in a queue, implemented as a linked list. When a running process is interrupted it goes to the waiting queue; when it finishes or aborts it is discarded.
Either way the dispatcher then selects a process from the queue to run.

Schedulers are special system software that handle process scheduling in various ways. Their main job is to select the jobs to submit into the system and to decide which process to run. There are three types: long-term, short-term and medium-term.

The long-term scheduler, also called the job scheduler, decides which programs are admitted to the system. It selects processes from the queue and loads them into memory. Its main aim is a balanced mix of jobs, I/O bound and processor bound, and it controls the degree of multiprogramming.
If that degree is stable, the average rate of process creation must equal the average rate of departure.
Time-sharing operating systems have no long-term scheduler. It is used when a process goes from new to ready.

The short-term scheduler, also called the CPU scheduler, aims to improve system performance by a chosen set of criteria. It changes a process from ready to running: it selects among the processes that are ready and gives the CPU to one of them.
Short-term schedulers, also known as dispatchers, decide which process to execute next, and are faster than long-term schedulers.

The medium-term scheduler is part of swapping. It removes processes from memory and so reduces the degree of multiprogramming; it handles swapped-out processes. A running process may become suspended if it makes an I/O request, and a suspended process cannot make progress.
To make space, the suspended process is moved to secondary storage. This is called swapping; the process is swapped out or rolled out.
Swapping may be necessary to improve the process mix. Later the medium-term scheduler can re-introduce the process so execution continues.
In short: long-term is a job scheduler, short-term a CPU scheduler, medium-term a swapping scheduler. The long-term is slowest and the short-term fastest, with the medium-term in between.
The long-term controls the degree of multiprogramming, the short-term gives little control over it, and the medium-term reduces it.

Now the context switch. It is the mechanism to store and restore the state, or context, of a CPU in the PCB so that a process can resume from the same point later. Using it, a single CPU can be shared by multiple processes.
Context switching is an essential feature of a multitasking operating system.

When the scheduler switches the CPU from one process to another, the state of the running process is stored in its PCB. Then the state of the next process is loaded from its own PCB and used to set the program counter, registers and so on. At that point the second process can start executing.
Context switches are computationally intensive, since register and memory state must be saved and restored. To reduce the time, some hardware uses two or more sets of processor registers.
What is stored: the program counter, scheduling information, base and limit register values, the currently used registers, the changed state, I/O state information and accounting information.

Because switching costs time with no useful work, the quantum should be long compared with the switch cost. The practice section asks you to compute the efficiency, which is the share of the CPU that does real work, and to move PCBs between queues.

summary: A process scheduler picks processes for the CPU with a scheduling algorithm. The tutorial covers six: first come first served, shortest job next, priority, shortest remaining time, round robin and multiple-level queues.

Non-preemptive algorithms let a process run until it finishes its allotted time; preemptive ones may take the CPU away, for example when a higher-priority or shorter job arrives, or when a quantum expires.

Shortest job next gives the lowest average waiting time but needs to know run times in advance. First come first served is simple but can make short jobs wait behind long ones. Round robin is fair and responsive but costs context switches.

items: A process scheduler assigns processes to the CPU based on a scheduling algorithm. The tutorial covers six: first come first served, shortest job next, priority scheduling, shortest remaining time, round robin and multiple-level queues.
These algorithms are either non-preemptive or preemptive. In non-preemptive algorithms, once a process enters the running state it cannot be preempted until it completes its allotted time.
Preemptive scheduling is based on priority: a scheduler may preempt a low-priority running process at any time when a high-priority process becomes ready.
A note on the examples before we start. The tutorial's wait-time tables come from figures with process tables that are not reproduced in the text, and some of their numbers do not match each other.
So in this course we use one consistent data set for every algorithm, which lets you compare them honestly.

The data set has four processes. P0 arrives at time 0 and needs 5 units. P1 arrives at 1 and needs 3. P2 arrives at 2 and needs 8. P3 arrives at 3 and needs 6. Waiting time here is the time a process spends ready but not running.

First come, first served, or FCFS. Jobs execute in order of arrival. It is non-preemptive, easy to understand and implement, and based on a FIFO queue. Its weakness is poor performance: the average wait is high.
On our data set: P0 runs 0 to 5, P1 5 to 8, P2 8 to 16, P3 16 to 22. Waiting times are 0, 4, 6 and 13, and the average is 5.75. The tutorial's table gives the same numbers for this case.

Shortest job next, SJN, also known as shortest job first. It is non-preemptive and the best approach to minimize waiting time. It is easy to implement in batch systems where the required CPU time is known in advance, and impossible in interactive systems where it is not known.

On our data set, at time 0 only P0 has arrived, so it runs 0 to 5. Then P1, P2 and P3 are all waiting; the shortest is P1 (3), then P3 (6), then P2 (8). Waiting times are 0, 4, 12 and 5, for an average of 5.25, better than FCFS.

Priority scheduling is a non-preemptive algorithm and one of the most common in batch systems. Each process is assigned a priority, and the highest priority runs first. Processes with the same priority run first come first served.
Priority can be decided from memory requirements, time requirements or any other resource requirement.
Shortest remaining time, SRT, is the preemptive version of SJN. The processor goes to the job closest to completion, but a newer ready job with a shorter time to completion can preempt it.
It is impossible when run time is unknown and is often used in batch environments where short jobs must be given preference.
On our data set the waiting times are 3, 0, 12 and 5, average 5.0. P1 preempts P0 at time 1.

Round robin is a preemptive algorithm. Each process gets a fixed time, the quantum. After running for that long it is preempted and another process runs. Context switching saves the states of preempted processes.
With a quantum of 3 on our data set the waiting times are 9, 2, 12 and 11, average 8.5, which is worse than the others but fair and responsive.

Multiple-level queues are not an independent algorithm. They use other algorithms to group and schedule jobs with common characteristics. Multiple queues are maintained, each with its own algorithm and a priority.
For example CPU-bound jobs go in one queue and I/O-bound jobs in another, and the scheduler alternately selects jobs from each queue.

The practice section implements four of these in Python and compares them. The Scheduler Gantt app lets you see the timelines. Note that the best average wait does not mean the best system: SJN can starve long jobs, and round robin trades waiting time for responsiveness.

practice.title: FCFS waiting times
practice.intro: Processes are [name, arrival, burst] in arrival order. Write fcfs_waits(procs): return the waiting time of each process, in input order, under first come first served. Waiting time = start time minus arrival time.
practice.hint: Keep a clock. start = max(clock, arrival); wait = start - arrival; clock = start + burst.
practice.solution:
def fcfs_waits(procs):
    t = 0
    waits = []
    for name, arrival, burst in procs:
        start = max(t, arrival)
        waits.append(start - arrival)
        t = start + burst
    return waits

practice.title: Shortest job next
practice.intro: Write sjn_waits(procs): the non-preemptive shortest job next waiting times, in input order. When the CPU is free, pick the arrived process with the smallest burst (ties: the earlier in the list). If nobody has arrived, jump the clock to the next arrival.
practice.hint: Loop until all are done. Among not-done processes with arrival <= clock choose min burst.
practice.solution:
def sjn_waits(procs):
    n = len(procs)
    done = [False] * n
    waits = [0] * n
    t = 0
    for _ in range(n):
        ready = [i for i in range(n) if not done[i] and procs[i][1] <= t]
        if not ready:
            t = min(procs[i][1] for i in range(n) if not done[i])
            ready = [i for i in range(n) if not done[i] and procs[i][1] <= t]
        i = min(ready, key=lambda k: (procs[k][2], k))
        waits[i] = t - procs[i][1]
        t += procs[i][2]
        done[i] = True
    return waits

practice.title: Round robin
practice.intro: Write rr_waits(procs, quantum): round robin waiting times in input order. Use a ready queue. A process that arrives while another runs joins the queue before the preempted process is put back at the end. Waiting time = finish time - arrival - burst.
practice.hint: Sort by arrival. Each step: take the first in the queue, run min(quantum, remaining), add newly arrived processes, then re-queue the preempted one.
practice.solution:
def rr_waits(procs, quantum):
    n = len(procs)
    rem = [p[2] for p in procs]
    order = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: (procs[i][1], i))
    queue = []
    nxt = 0
    t = 0
    finish = [0] * n
    done = 0
    while done < n:
        while nxt < n and procs[order[nxt]][1] <= t:
            queue.append(order[nxt])
            nxt += 1
        if not queue:
            t = procs[order[nxt]][1]
            continue
        i = queue.pop(0)
        run = min(quantum, rem[i])
        t += run
        rem[i] -= run
        while nxt < n and procs[order[nxt]][1] <= t:
            queue.append(order[nxt])
            nxt += 1
        if rem[i] > 0:
            queue.append(i)
        else:
            finish[i] = t
            done += 1
    return [finish[i] - procs[i][1] - procs[i][2] for i in range(n)]

practice.title: Shortest remaining time
practice.intro: Write srt_waits(procs): preemptive shortest remaining time, simulated one time unit at a time. At each tick run the arrived, unfinished process with the least remaining time (ties: earlier in the list). Return waiting times in input order (finish - arrival - burst).
practice.hint: Loop with t from 0. Build the list of ready processes, take min by (remaining, index), reduce its remaining by 1, and record the finish time when it reaches 0.
practice.solution:
def srt_waits(procs):
    n = len(procs)
    rem = [p[2] for p in procs]
    finish = [0] * n
    t = 0
    left = n
    while left:
        ready = [i for i in range(n) if rem[i] > 0 and procs[i][1] <= t]
        if not ready:
            t += 1
            continue
        i = min(ready, key=lambda k: (rem[k], k))
        rem[i] -= 1
        t += 1
        if rem[i] == 0:
            finish[i] = t
            left -= 1
    return [finish[i] - procs[i][1] - procs[i][2] for i in range(n)]

summary: A thread is a flow of execution through the process code with its own program counter, registers and stack. Threads of one process share the code segment, data segment and open files, so one thread's change to shared memory is seen by all.

Threads are lightweight: cheaper to create and switch than processes, and they let one process do several things at once. The price is that threads can read and write each other's data, so they must coordinate.

Threads are implemented at user level, by a library, or at kernel level, by the OS. Models map user threads to kernel threads many-to-one, one-to-one or many-to-many, trading concurrency against cost.

glossary.def: A flow of execution through process code with its own program counter, registers and stack.
Another name for a thread; it uses fewer resources than a classical process.
A thread managed by a thread library in user space; the kernel does not know about it.

keyPoints: A thread has its own program counter, registers and stack, and shares code, data and open files with its peers.
Each thread belongs to exactly one process.
Thread switching needs less OS interaction than process switching.
User threads: fast to create, but a blocking call can block the whole process and they cannot use multiple processors.
Kernel threads: can run in parallel and one can block without blocking others, but are slower to create.
Many-to-one, one-to-one and many-to-many are the three mapping models.

items: A thread is a flow of execution through the process code. It has its own program counter that tracks which instruction to execute next, system registers that hold its current working variables, and a stack that holds its execution history.

A thread shares a few things with its peer threads: the code segment, the data segment and open files. When one thread alters a memory item in the shared segment, all other threads see it. A thread is also called a lightweight process.
Threads improve performance through parallelism and by reducing overhead.

Each thread belongs to exactly one process, and no thread can exist outside a process. Each thread represents a separate flow of control. Threads are used successfully in network servers and web servers, and they provide a good foundation for parallel execution on shared-memory multiprocessors.

How do processes and threads differ? A process is heavyweight and resource intensive; a thread is lightweight and takes fewer resources. Switching processes needs interaction with the OS; switching threads does not need that.

In a multiple-process environment each process has its own memory and file resources, while threads share open files and child processes. If one process is blocked, no other process of that task can run, whereas while one thread waits another thread of the same task can run.
And a risk: processes operate independently of one another, but one thread can read, write or change another thread's data. That is why threads need coordination.

The advantages of threads: they minimize context switching time, give concurrency within a process, offer efficient communication, are more economical to create and switch, and let an application make better use of multiprocessor architectures.
Threads are implemented in two ways. User-level threads are managed by the user, through a thread library. Kernel-level threads are managed by the operating system, acting on the kernel.

With user-level threads the kernel does not know threads exist. The thread library contains code to create and destroy threads, pass messages and data between them, schedule them and save and restore their contexts. The application starts with a single thread.

User-level threads have advantages. Thread switching does not need kernel mode privileges. They can run on any operating system. Scheduling can be application specific. They are fast to create and manage.
The disadvantages: in a typical OS most system calls are blocking, so one blocking call can stop the whole process, and a multithreaded application cannot use multiple processors.

With kernel-level threads, the kernel does thread management and there is no thread-management code in the application. The kernel keeps context information for the process as a whole and for each thread, and schedules on a thread basis.
Any application can be multithreaded, with all of its threads in one process.

Advantages of kernel threads: the kernel can schedule multiple threads of one process on multiple processors at the same time; if one thread blocks, the kernel can schedule another from the same process; and kernel routines themselves can be multithreaded.
Disadvantages: they are slower to create and manage, and transfer of control between threads in a process requires a switch into kernel mode.

Some operating systems combine both. Solaris is the tutorial's example. In a combined system threads of one application can run in parallel on multiple processors and a blocking call need not block the whole process. There are three models.

Many-to-many multiplexes any number of user threads onto an equal or smaller number of kernel threads. Developers can create as many user threads as they need, and the kernel threads can run in parallel on a multiprocessor. When a thread makes a blocking call, the kernel can schedule another.

Many-to-one maps many user threads to one kernel thread. The thread library manages them in user space. When a thread makes a blocking system call the entire process blocks, and only one thread can access the kernel at a time, so threads cannot run in parallel on multiprocessors.

One-to-one maps each user thread to a kernel thread. It gives more concurrency than many-to-one, allows another thread to run when one blocks, and supports parallel execution on multiprocessors. The disadvantage is that creating a user thread needs a kernel thread.
The tutorial notes that OS/2, Windows NT and Windows 2000 use one-to-one.

The danger of shared data deserves a demonstration. If two threads both do counter = counter + 1, each does three steps: load the counter into a register, add one, store it back. If the steps interleave badly, an update is lost.
The practice section lets you replay an interleaving and see the result.

summary: Memory management handles primary memory and moves processes between main memory and disk. It tracks every memory location, decides which process gets memory and when, and updates the status when memory is freed.
Programs use logical addresses; the memory management unit translates them to physical addresses at run time.
Memory can be allocated in single or multiple partitions, which leads to fragmentation: external, when free space is split into unusable pieces, and internal, when a block is larger than needed.
Paging splits a process into fixed-size pages loaded into fixed-size frames, avoiding external fragmentation. Segmentation splits a process into variable-size segments that match program modules.

A location in main memory; the set of them is the physical address space.

keyPoints: Symbolic addresses become relative at compile time and physical at load time.
Compile-time and load-time binding give identical virtual and physical addresses; execution-time binding does not.
The MMU translates logical to physical addresses at run time.
Static linking combines modules into one program; dynamic linking keeps a reference resolved at run time.
Fragmentation: external (enough space, not contiguous) and internal (block bigger than needed).
Paging: pages and frames same size, page table, offset stays the same. Segmentation: variable-size segments with base and length.

items: Memory management is the function of an operating system that handles primary memory and moves processes back and forth between main memory and disk during execution. It keeps track of every memory location, whether allocated or free.
It checks how much memory to allocate, decides which process gets memory and when, and updates the status when memory is freed.

The process address space is the set of logical addresses a process references in its code. With 32-bit addressing, addresses range from 0 to 0x7fffffff, which is 2 to the 31st power possible numbers, a theoretical size of 2 gigabytes.
The OS maps logical addresses to physical addresses when memory is allocated.

There are three kinds of addresses. Symbolic addresses are used in source code: variable names, constants and instruction labels. A compiler converts them into relative addresses. The loader generates the physical addresses when the program is loaded into main memory.

Virtual and physical addresses are the same under compile-time and load-time address binding. They differ under execution-time binding. The set of all logical addresses is the logical address space; the set of corresponding physical addresses is the physical address space.
The run-time mapping from virtual to physical addresses is done by the memory management unit, the MMU, a hardware device.

Next, loading and linking. With static loading the whole program is loaded into memory before it starts. With dynamic loading, routines are stored on disk in relocatable form and loaded only when the program needs them.
Static linking combines all needed modules into one executable to avoid run-time dependency.
With dynamic linking the program only holds a reference to the module and the rest is resolved at run time. Dynamic link libraries, DLLs, on Windows and shared objects on Unix are examples.
Swapping is a mechanism where a process is swapped temporarily out of main memory to secondary storage, making memory available to others. Later the system swaps it back.
Swapping affects performance, but it lets the system run multiple and big processes in parallel, which is why it is also described as a technique for memory compaction.

The total swap time includes moving the process to disk, copying it back, and the time to regain memory. Here is a worked example, with a correction. A process of 2048 KB on a disk transferring about 1 MB per second: 2048 KB divided by 1024 KB per second is 2 seconds, one way.
The tutorial writes this as 200 milliseconds, which is a slip; 2 seconds is 2000 milliseconds. Swapping in and out takes about 4 seconds, plus overhead.

Memory allocation. Main memory has two partitions: low memory, where the operating system resides, and high memory, where user processes are held. In single-partition allocation a relocation register holds the smallest physical address and a limit register holds the range of logical addresses.
Every logical address must be less than the limit register. This protects processes from each other and from changing OS code and data.

In multiple-partition allocation, main memory is divided into a number of fixed-size partitions, each holding one process. When a partition is free, a process is selected from the input queue and loaded into it. When the process terminates, the partition becomes available again.

Fragmentation. As processes are loaded and removed, free memory is broken into little pieces. Eventually processes cannot be placed in blocks that are too small. There are two kinds. External fragmentation: total free space is enough, but it is not contiguous.
Internal fragmentation: the block assigned is bigger than needed, and the unused part cannot be used by another process.

External fragmentation can be reduced by compaction, shuffling memory contents so free memory forms one large block. To make compaction possible, relocation must be dynamic. Internal fragmentation can be reduced by assigning the smallest partition that is still large enough for the process.

Paging. Paging breaks the process address space into blocks of the same size called pages, with sizes a power of 2, between 512 and 8192 bytes. Main memory is divided into fixed-size frames, the same size as pages, so there is no external fragmentation.
A page-map table records which frame holds each page.

Address translation. A logical address is a page number plus a page offset. A physical address is a frame number plus the same offset. The system gives the page a frame and records it in the page table.
When memory runs out, the OS moves idle pages to secondary memory and brings them back when needed.

lesson.tex: \begin{gathered} \text{physical address} = \text{frame}(p) \times \text{page size} + d \\[0.6em] \text{where } p = \lfloor a / \text{page size} \rfloor,\; d = a \bmod \text{page size} \end{gathered}

items: Paging reduces external fragmentation but still has internal fragmentation, because the last page may be partly empty. It is simple and efficient, and swapping is easy because pages and frames are equal in size. The page table needs extra memory, which hurts small-RAM systems.

Segmentation divides each job into segments of different sizes, one for each module of related functions. Each segment is its own logical address space. Segments are loaded into non-contiguous memory, but each segment sits in a contiguous block.
It works like paging, but segments have variable length, while pages are fixed.
The OS keeps a segment map table per process, storing for each segment its starting address and length. A reference gives a segment number and an offset.
The practice section has you implement the relocation and limit check, the three classic placement strategies, page-table translation and the swap-time calculation.

summary: Virtual memory lets a computer address more memory than is physically installed by using disk to emulate RAM. Programs can be larger than physical memory, and each virtual address is translated, which also gives memory protection.

It is usually implemented by demand paging: pages are loaded only when referenced. Referencing a page that is not in memory causes a page fault, and the OS brings the page in, possibly replacing another page.

A page replacement algorithm decides which page to evict. FIFO evicts the oldest, optimal evicts the one used furthest in the future, LRU evicts the least recently used, and LFU and MFU use counts. Algorithms are compared by their page faults on a reference string.

glossary.def: A section of disk set up to emulate RAM so programs can be larger than physical memory.
Loading pages only when they are referenced, not in advance.
A reference to a page that is not in main memory, handled by the OS.
The policy that decides which page to swap out when a frame is needed.

keyPoints: Virtual memory extends physical memory using disk and provides protection.
Not all of a program is needed at once: error routines, rare features, tables with unused space.
Demand paging loads on reference; a page fault transfers control to the OS.
Quality of a replacement algorithm: less time waiting for page-ins is better.
OPT has the lowest fault rate; LRU is a good practical approximation.
Evaluate with a reference string and count page faults.

items: A computer can address more memory than the amount physically installed. The extra memory is called virtual memory, a section of the hard disk set up to emulate the computer's RAM. The visible advantage is that programs can be larger than physical memory.
Virtual memory serves two purposes. First, it extends physical memory by using disk. Second, it gives memory protection, because each virtual address is translated into a physical address.

The entire program does not need to be in memory when: error-handling routines are used only when an error occurs; certain options are rarely used; and many tables are assigned a fixed address space of which only a little is used.

Running a program that is only partly in memory has many benefits. Fewer I/O operations are needed to load or swap a user program. A program is no longer limited by physical memory. Each program takes less physical memory, so more programs can run at once, increasing CPU utilization and throughput.
In general-purpose microprocessors a memory management unit, the MMU, is built into the hardware. Its job is to translate virtual addresses into physical addresses.
Virtual memory is commonly implemented by demand paging; it can also be implemented in a segmentation system, called demand segmentation.

Demand paging is like paging with swapping, where processes reside in secondary memory and pages are loaded only on demand, not in advance. On a context switch the OS does not copy the old program's pages out or the new program's pages in.
It simply starts the new program after loading its first page and fetches other pages as they are referenced.

If the program references a page that is not in main memory, because it was swapped out a little ago, the processor treats this invalid reference as a page fault. It transfers control from the program to the OS, which demands the page back into memory.

Advantages of demand paging: a large virtual memory, more efficient use of memory, and no limit on the degree of multiprogramming. The disadvantage is the larger number of tables and the processor overhead for handling page interrupts.

Page replacement algorithms are the techniques the OS uses to decide which memory pages to swap out, writing them to disk, when a page must be allocated. Paging happens whenever a page fault occurs and a free page cannot be used.
If the replaced page is referenced again it must be read from disk, which needs I/O. That determines the quality of the algorithm: the less time spent waiting for page-ins, the better.
The algorithm tries to minimize the total number of page misses, balanced against the cost of storage and processor time for the algorithm itself.

We evaluate an algorithm by running it on a particular string of memory references and counting page faults. This string is the reference string. For a given page size we only need the page number, not the entire address.
And if page p is referenced, any immediately following references to p will not fault.
Example: the address sequence 123, 215, 600, 1234, 76, 96 with a page size of 100 gives the reference string 1, 2, 6, 12, 0, 0.
First in, first out: the oldest page in main memory is replaced. It is easy to implement: keep a list, replace pages from the tail and add new pages at the head.

Optimal page replacement has the lowest page-fault rate of all algorithms. It is called OPT or MIN. It replaces the page that will not be used for the longest period of time. It cannot be implemented in a real system, because it needs the future, but it is the benchmark.

Least recently used: the page that has not been used for the longest time in main memory is replaced. It is easy to implement: keep a list and look back into time. Page buffering keeps a pool of free frames.
On a fault, a page is selected, the new page is written into a free frame, the page table is updated and the process restarts; the dirty victim is written to disk afterwards.

Least frequently used replaces the page with the smallest count, but suffers when a page is used heavily early and never again. Most frequently used is based on the argument that the page with the smallest count was probably just brought in and has yet to be used.

On the classic reference string 7, 0, 1, 2, 0, 3, 0, 4, 2, 3, 0, 3, 2, 1, 2, 0, 1, 7, 0, 1 with three frames, FIFO has 15 faults, LRU 12 and OPT 9. You can check those numbers in the practice section.
FIFO even has a surprise called Belady's anomaly: on 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 it faults 9 times with 3 frames and 10 times with 4.

summary: One of the OS's jobs is to manage devices. I/O devices are block devices, character devices or network-like devices, and each is attached to the computer through a controller.
The CPU talks to a device by memory-mapped I/O, special I/O instructions or direct memory access. Polling keeps the CPU busy checking a status bit; interrupts let the device signal when it is done.
With DMA, a controller moves a whole block between the device and memory and interrupts the CPU once, which saves one interrupt per word.

glossary.def: A device that stores data in fixed-size blocks, each addressable. A disk is an example.
A device that delivers or accepts a stream of characters, such as a keyboard or serial port.
The electronic part that operates a device and connects it to the computer.
The CPU repeatedly checks a status bit to see if the device is ready.
A signal from a device that makes the CPU stop and run a handler.
Direct memory access: a controller transfers data between memory and a device without CPU involvement per word.
Device registers share the memory address space and are read and written like memory.

keyPoints: Block devices: fixed blocks, random access. Character devices: streams, no addressing.
Controllers hide device details from the OS.
Polling is simple but wastes CPU time.
Interrupts let the CPU do other work while the device operates.
DMA: one interrupt per block rather than per word.
Memory-mapped I/O avoids special instructions.

items: One of the important jobs of an operating system is to manage various I/O devices, including mouse, keyboards, touch pad, disk drives, display adapters, USB devices, bit-mapped screens, LEDs, analog-to-digital converters, on/off switches, network connections, audio I/O, printers and more.

An I/O system is required to take an application's I/O request and send it to the physical device, then take whatever response comes back and send it to the application. I/O devices can be divided into two broad categories.

Block devices store data in fixed-size blocks, usually 512 bytes to 32 kilobytes, and each block has its own address. Transfers are in whole blocks, and the device can read any block independently of others. Hard disks, USB cameras and Blu-ray discs are examples.
Character devices deliver or accept a stream of characters with no block structure. They are not addressable and have no seek operation. Examples are printers, network interfaces, mice and keyboards.
Device drivers are software modules that can be plugged into an OS to handle a particular device. The OS takes help from them to handle all I/O devices.

The device controller works like an interface between a device and the device driver. I/O units, keyboard and mouse, generally have a mechanical component and an electronic component, and the electronic component is the device controller.
There is always a device controller and a device driver for each device so the two can communicate.

There are several ways to talk to a device. One is the special I/O instruction. It usually specifies a byte or word to transfer and a port number that selects the device. The CPU does the work itself, so it ties up the processor while the transfer happens.
Memory-mapped I/O. The device registers are mapped into the address space of the CPU, so reading and writing them is the same as reading and writing memory, and no special instructions are needed.
The disadvantage is that a cache must be disabled for the device addresses, or it will hold stale values.
The CPU can also learn the status of a device by polling. It repeatedly reads a status register until a ready bit is set. That wastes CPU time, because the processor is busy waiting.
The alternative is interrupts: the device sends a signal when it is ready, and the CPU runs an interrupt handler, then returns to the interrupted work.
Interrupt-driven I/O has a cost per word when moving large amounts of data. Direct memory access fixes this. A DMA controller is given the memory address, the count and the direction.
It moves the whole block between device and memory by itself, stealing bus cycles from the CPU, and raises one interrupt when the whole transfer is done.

Here are the numbers. Transferring a 4096-byte block with a 4-byte word and one interrupt per word needs 1024 interrupts. With DMA it needs one. The practice section lets you count and compare polling cost too.

summary: I/O software is organized in layers: interrupt handlers at the bottom, then device drivers, then device-independent OS software, then user-level libraries. Each layer hides details from the one above.
Device drivers contain the device-specific code. The device-independent layer gives uniform naming, buffering, error reporting, allocation and protection.

Three ideas smooth device speed differences: buffering holds data in memory during a transfer, caching keeps copies in faster memory, and spooling queues jobs for a device like a printer that cannot share.

items: I/O software is often organized in layers. From the bottom: interrupt handlers, device drivers, device-independent operating system software, and user-level software. Each layer has a well-defined function and interface to its neighbours.

Device drivers are software modules that can be plugged into an OS to handle a particular device. The operating system takes help from device drivers to handle all I/O devices. A driver encapsulates device-dependent code and accepts abstract commands, such as read block n, from the layer above.
A device driver issues commands to the controller, then either blocks until an interrupt arrives or checks status itself.

Its tasks include accepting requests from the layer above, checking input parameters, translating abstract requests into concrete ones, checking whether the device is in use, issuing commands, and checking for errors.

The interrupt handler is the lowest layer. Interrupts are unpleasant, but hidden. The best way is to block the driver that started an I/O operation until the I/O completes and the interrupt occurs. The handler saves registers, services the interrupt, wakes the blocked driver and restores state.

Device-independent I/O software does functions common to all devices. Its main functions: uniform interfacing for drivers, buffering, error reporting, allocating and releasing dedicated devices, and providing a device-independent block size.
For example, a disk read of a block is the same request to the OS whichever disk it is.

User-space I/O software is the layer of library procedures such as printf or read, and spooling systems. Library procedures format data, and make system calls. Spooling is a way to deal with dedicated devices in a multiprogramming system.

Take the printer. Though it is possible to let a process open its special file directly, a process could hog it for hours. Instead, a special process called a daemon is created, with a special directory called the spooling directory.
To print a file, a process first generates the file, then puts it in the spooling directory. The daemon is the only process allowed to use the printer.
Buffering stores data temporarily while it is transferred between two devices, or between a device and an application.
Reasons for buffering: coping with a speed mismatch between producer and consumer, adapting to devices with different transfer sizes, and maintaining copy semantics for application I/O.

Caching is a different idea. A cache is a region of fast memory that holds a copy of data. Access to the cached copy is more efficient than access to the original. A buffer may hold the only existing copy of a data item, whereas a cache just holds a copy on faster storage.
I/O can also be synchronous or asynchronous. With synchronous I/O the process waits until the operation is complete. With asynchronous I/O the process carries on and is notified later.
The practice section has you build the bounded buffer between a producer and a consumer, and a spool queue for a printer.

    out = []
    for name, arrival, pages in jobs:

        t = start + pages
        out.append([name, t])
    return out

summary: A file is a named collection of related information on secondary storage. The file system gives users a way to name, organize, store, retrieve and protect files, and maps files onto disk blocks.
Files have attributes such as name, type, location, size, protection and time. Directories organize files, and access is sequential or direct.
Three ways to allocate disk blocks: contiguous, linked and indexed. Each trades speed, fragmentation and random access differently.

glossary.def: A named collection of related information recorded on secondary storage.
The part of the OS that names, stores, organizes and protects files.
A structure that holds information about files.

A file occupies a set of adjacent blocks.
Each block holds a pointer to the next block of the file.
An index block lists all the blocks of the file.

keyPoints: File attributes: name, type, location, size, protection, time and date.
File types: ordinary, directory and special files.
Contiguous: fast direct access, external fragmentation, files hard to grow.
Linked: no external fragmentation, slow direct access, pointers lost if damaged.
Indexed: supports direct access, needs an index block.
Free space can be tracked with a bit map or a linked list.

items: A file is a named collection of related information that is recorded on secondary storage such as magnetic disks, magnetic tapes and optical disks. In general a file is a sequence of bits, bytes, lines or records, whose meaning is defined by the file's creator and user.

File structure. A file has a structure that depends on its type. A text file is a sequence of characters organized into lines. A source file is a sequence of procedures and functions. An object file is a sequence of bytes organized into blocks understandable by the machine.
The OS decides the structure when the file is created.

File type refers to the ability of the OS to distinguish different types of file, such as text files and source files and binary files. Many operating systems support many types of files. They fall into three categories. Ordinary files hold user information, usually ASCII or binary.
Directory files contain information about other files. Special files are device files and hold no data.

The file system maintains attributes for each file: the name, which is kept in human-readable form; the type; the location of the device and place on disk; the size; the protection, who may read, write or execute; and the time, date and user identification, useful for protection, security and usage monitoring.

Directory structure. A directory is a way to organize files. The simplest is a single-level directory, where all files are in one place. It is easy to support but has naming problems: names must be unique. A two-level directory gives each user a directory.
A tree-structured directory allows users to create their own subdirectories.

Access methods. Sequential access reads records one after another, as on tape. Direct access, also called relative access, lets a program read or write blocks in any order, using the block number. Disks make direct access possible, and databases use it a great deal.

Now allocation. The disk is divided into blocks, and the file system decides which blocks to give a file. In contiguous allocation each file occupies a set of contiguous blocks. The directory needs only the starting block and the length. It supports sequential and direct access easily.
The problems: external fragmentation, and files are difficult to grow.

In linked allocation each file is a linked list of disk blocks that may be scattered anywhere on disk. The directory stores pointers to the first and last blocks, and each block contains a pointer to the next. There is no external fragmentation and files can grow easily.
But direct access is inefficient, because to reach block i you follow i pointers, and a damaged pointer loses the rest of the file.
In indexed allocation all the pointers are brought together into one index block. Each file has its own index block, an array of disk block addresses; entry i points to block i of the file.
It supports direct access without external fragmentation, but the index block takes space, and small files waste most of it.

Free space management. The system must know which blocks are free. A bit map has one bit per block, for example 1 for free, and the first free block is found by scanning for a set bit. A free list links the free blocks together. Grouping and counting are refinements.
In practice you can compute the block a byte lives in, follow a linked chain, and allocate a contiguous run. That is what the practice section asks you to code.

practice.title: Follow a linked file
practice.intro: A linked file's blocks are in a table: next[b] is the block after b, and -1 ends the file. Write linked_blocks(next_table, start, n): return the first n blocks of the file, starting at block start, or the whole file if it is shorter than n.
practice.hint: Start at block b = start. While b != -1 and fewer than n collected: append b and set b = next[b].
practice.solution:
def linked_blocks(next_table, start, n):
    out = []
    b = start
    while b != -1 and len(out) < n:
        out.append(b)
        b = next_table[b]
    return out

summary: Security means protecting the system's resources from unauthorized access. Operating system security measures include authentication, one-time passwords, and monitoring against program and system threats.
Authentication proves the user's identity by something they know, have or are. One-time passwords protect against replay of captured passwords.

Threats include trojan horses, trap doors, worms, viruses and denial of service. Defences include least privilege, monitoring, and a trusted computing base, rated in classes from D (minimal) up to A (verified design).

glossary.def: Verifying the identity of a user or process.
A password valid for one use only, so a captured password is useless later.
A program that appears useful but performs hidden harmful actions.
A hidden entry point left in a program that bypasses normal security.
Code that does harm only when a condition occurs.
Code that attaches to other programs and replicates.
A program that copies itself across a network without needing a host program.
Giving each user or process only the access it needs.
A table of subjects by objects with the rights each subject holds.

keyPoints: Security covers authentication, one-time passwords, and defence against program and system threats.
Authentication factors: what you know, have or are.
Program threats: trojan horse, trap door, logic bomb, buffer overflow.
System threats: worms, viruses, denial of service.
Computer security classes: D, C1, C2, B1, B2, B3, A.
Least privilege limits damage.

items: Security refers to providing a protection system to computer system resources such as the CPU, memory, disk, software programs and, most importantly, the data and information stored in the system.
If a computer program is run by an unauthorized user, he or she may cause severe damage to the computer or its data.

Security can be addressed by two means: authentication and one-time passwords. And the operating system must monitor for program threats and system threats. Authentication refers to identifying each user of the system and associating the executing programs with those users.
It is the OS's responsibility to create a protection system that ensures a user who runs a particular program is authentic.

Operating systems generally identify users in three ways. Username and password: the user enters a registered name and a password, which the system checks. User card or key: the user must punch a card in a slot or enter a key produced by a key generator.
User attribute, such as a fingerprint, eye retina pattern or signature.

One-time passwords provide additional security along with normal authentication. In a one-time password system, a unique password is required every time a user tries to log in. Once used, the password cannot be used again.

They are implemented in various ways: random numbers, where the user gets cards with numbers printed with corresponding letters; a secret key, where the user gets a hardware device that creates a secret id mapped to the user id; and a network password, where the system sends a password by email or text to the user.

Now program threats. If a user program makes processes do malicious tasks, it is known as a program threat. A common example is a Trojan horse: a code segment that misuses its environment, for example a program that appears to be a login but steals the password.
A trap door is a hole left by the program's author so that he or she can bypass the security. Programs with trap doors are hard to detect.
A logic bomb is a program that misbehaves only when certain conditions are met, otherwise it works as a genuine program. It is hard to detect.
And there is the stack and buffer overflow: an exploit that enters more data than a buffer can hold, so the extra data overwrites neighbouring memory and may run attacker code.

System threats refer to misuse of system services and network connections to put the user in trouble. They can be used to launch program threats on a complete network, called a program attack. System threats create an environment in which operating system resources and user files are misused.

A worm is a process that can choke a system's performance by using system resources to extreme levels. It generates multiple copies of itself, each using resources and preventing other processes from getting any. Worms can shut down a whole network.
Ports scanning is a mechanism by which a cracker tries to detect system vulnerabilities. Denial of service attacks stop users from legitimate use of the system, usually by overloading it.

A virus loads itself into a computer system and attaches to a program. Unlike a worm it needs a host. Its aim is to modify or destroy files and make programs misbehave. Defence includes least privilege, antivirus software, and being careful with downloads and attachments.

Computer security classifications. The US Department of Defense Trusted Computer System Evaluation Criteria specifies four security divisions. Type A is the highest, with verified design, and Type B and C are in the middle. Type D is minimal protection.

Class B1 gives labelled protection, B2 structured protection, B3 security domains. C1 is discretionary security protection and C2 is controlled access protection, with auditing and accountability. D is for systems that failed higher evaluation, like DOS.

The practice section codes a one-time password check, an access-matrix lookup and a threat classifier. It also asks you to rank security classes. These are small, but they show the logic that real systems use.

summary: Linux is a popular open source Unix-like operating system whose kernel was written by Linus Torvalds. Its main parts are the kernel, system libraries and system utilities.
The kernel runs in kernel mode with full access to hardware; utilities and applications run in user mode. System libraries are standard functions applications use to reach the kernel.

Key features are portability, open source, multiuser and multiprogramming support, a hierarchical file system, a shell and security. The architecture has four layers: hardware, kernel, shell and utilities.

glossary.def: An open source Unix-like operating system built around the Linux kernel.
The core of the OS. It abstracts hardware, manages memory, processes and devices, and runs in kernel mode.
Special functions through which applications reach kernel features without needing kernel code access rights.
A program performing a specialized task, such as listing processes or managing files.
The privileged mode with unrestricted access to hardware and memory.
The restricted mode in which applications run.

keyPoints: Linux has a kernel, system libraries and system utilities.
The kernel runs in kernel mode; applications and utilities run in user mode.
Features: portable, open source, multiuser, multiprogramming, hierarchical file system, shell, security.
Layers: hardware, kernel, shell, utilities.
The shell turns commands into kernel requests.
Everything is a file: devices are files in the file system.

items: Linux is one of the popular versions of the UNIX operating system. It is open source, as its source code is freely available, and it is free to use. Linux was designed with UNIX compatibility in mind, and its functionality list is quite similar to that of UNIX.
The Linux operating system has three major components. The kernel is the core part and abstracts the hardware: it consists of all the code that needs to run in kernel mode.

System libraries are special functions or programs that application programs and system utilities use to access the kernel's features. System utilities are programs responsible for individual, specialized tasks.

Kernel code executes in kernel mode. Kernel mode has full access to all the resources of the computer. This code represents a single process, executes in a single address space, and does not require any context switch, which is why it is very efficient and fast.
The kernel runs each process and provides system services, plus protected access to hardware.

Support code that is not required to run in kernel mode is in the system libraries. User programs and other system programs work in user mode, which has no direct access to system hardware or kernel code. They use the system libraries to call kernel functions to perform low-level tasks.

The kernel is also modular: loadable kernel modules can be added or removed while the system runs. A module typically implements a device driver, a file system or a networking protocol. This keeps the core small and lets new hardware be supported without rebuilding the kernel.
Linux has basic features. It is portable, working on different hardware platforms. It is open source, with a community developing and enhancing it. It is multiuser and supports multiprogramming.

It has a hierarchical file system with a standard directory structure, and a shell, a command interpreter, that can run external programs. It includes security with authentication, access control and encryption.

Architecture. Linux has four layers. The hardware layer is made of all peripheral devices: RAM, hard disk, CPU and so on. The kernel is the core and interacts directly with hardware, and hides low-level details from system and application programs.
The shell is an interface to the kernel; it takes commands from the user and executes the kernel's functions. Utilities provide the functionality of the operating system to the user.

In Linux, nearly everything is a file, including devices. That is why the same open, read and write system calls work for a disk file, a terminal or a pipe. In the file system the top is a single root directory, written with a slash, and directories such as bin, etc, home and dev hang below it.

A shell session shows the pieces. A command like ps lists processes, using kernel data. The practice section gives you a scripted Linux terminal and a Python parser that reads the output of ps. This ties the course together: processes, memory, files and devices all appear in one place.

That is the course. To review: processes are programs in execution described by PCBs and moved among queues; schedulers choose who runs; memory management, paging and virtual memory give each process a private view; I/O software and file systems hide devices behind files; and security protects all of it. Linux is one real system that puts these ideas to work.
